# Quarto that renders while you type.

::: {.lead}
Quarto Hub is a Quarto editor in the browser with no render step. You write in the source or directly in the rendered page, and either way it's the same `.qmd`. When you want input, you share a link: teammates and agents edit and comment in your project, not in a PDF someone emailed back.

Today Hub is for markdown: websites, notes, slides. Code cells are next. Nothing about quarto-cli changes.
:::

::: {.hero-actions}
[Open Hub](https://quarto-hub.com){.btn .btn-primary .btn-lg role="button"}

<span class="eyebrow" style="margin-top:2.5rem">Why</span>

## Code and prose belong in one document. So do the people.

Quarto's premise is that analysis and writing are one artifact, in plain text you can version. What plain text never had is the other half of Google Docs: several people in the same document at once, comments where the words are, no one waiting for a render or a pull request. Hub adds that half without giving up the source.

:::

::: {.alt-background}
::: {.content-block}

<span class="eyebrow">Today</span>

## What works today

::: {.card-grid .four}
::: {.hub-card}
### Websites and docs
The whole project: file tree, outline, every page rendered as you edit it.
:::
::: {.hub-card}
### Meeting notes
One `.qmd` the whole team types into during the call. It's rendered before the call ends.
:::
::: {.hub-card}
### Slides
revealjs decks, edited and previewed in place. Your co-presenter gets the link, not a PDF.
:::
::: {.hub-card}
### Agents
Point Claude or any MCP client at the project. It edits the same files you do, and every change stays in the history. Early, and improving.
:::
:::

Anyone with the link can open the project, read it, and comment. They don't need an account or a Quarto install. You sign in with Google to create and own projects.

:::
:::

<span class="eyebrow">Built on Quarto 2</span>

## The engine underneath

Rendering on every keystroke takes a much faster Quarto. That is Quarto 2: the engine rewritten in Rust, an order of magnitude faster than Quarto 1, and small enough to run inside the browser tab. You don't install it to use Hub; it's already there.

Quarto 2 is experimental right now, and it is the path forward. quarto-cli stays supported, and over time more of what you do there will work in Quarto 2.
